content.title: Field test reveals 3500-year-old Mycenaean armor is battle-worthy
content.text: Greece: Marines test 3500-year-old Mycenaean armor, find it battle-worthyInitially considered ceremonial, the Dendra armor has now been labeled as suitable for combat after being tested by marine volunteers. A suit of armor dating back to the later Bronze Age civilization in Greece represented by finds at Mycenae has entered the spotlight again, this time it has been deemed suitable for extendable combat. The infamous Mycenaean “Dendra armor” which is attributed as the oldest intact full-set of body armor in human history is one of the most prominently known military technological achievements. This armor was tested by volunteers from the Marines of the Hellenic Armed Forces in a study conducted by Andreas Flouris of the University of Thessaly, Greece. Initially considered ceremonial, the Dendra armor has been now tagged as suitable for combat. Comprehending nature of warfare in Late Bronze Age Europe The Mycenaean armor dates back 3500 years discovered near the village of Dendra in 1960 shed light on the nature of warfare in Late Bronze Age Europe. As per Hellenic Armors, the Dendra armor was unearthed by the Greco-Swedish expedition at the territory of Dendra village in the Argolida region (Peloponnese, Greece). This was a facet of the findings which included the Mycenean Tomb number 12 (the final resting place of a local Warlord). Researchers combined historical and experimental evidence to assess the combat suitability of the Dendra armor. They developed a simulated Bronze Age combat protocol based on historical accounts from Homer’s Iliad and other physiological and environmental evidence. Thirteen volunteers from the Marines of the Hellenic Armed Forces were equipped with replicas of the Dendra armor and Bronze Age weapons and underwent an eleven-hour combat simulation. Dendra armor is battle-worthy The results revealed that armor did not actually impede the warriors’ fighting abilities nor did it cause severe strain on the bodies, leading scientists to believe it worthy of battle. The study’s authors also devised software to simulate combat conditions, allowing for more varied scenario testing of the armor’s efficacy. According to a statement by the scientists, the combat simulation was developed based on historical accounts from Homer’s Iliad along with additional physiological and environmental evidence to create an approximation of typical diet, activities, and maneuvers of the Mycenaean military. “The “Dendra” armor can be considered as a unique Universal monument of human civilization and human technological progress,” stated the Hellenic Armors. “It is a “window” to the heart of the Mycenean world, a Megalithic moving lethal structure that reflects the passion of the people of that era for perfection, for domination, for progress.” “The experiment found that the replicated Dendra armor did not limit a warrior’s fighting ability or cause severe strain on the wearer,” scientists iterated in the statement. “These results suggest that the Dendra armor was battle-worthy, implying that the Mycenaean’s powerful impact in Mediterranean history was due partly to their armor technology,” they added. The new software to simulate combat conditions paved the way for testing the armor’s effectiveness in different scenarios. This tool, along with further research aims to enhance the comprehension of Mycenaean combat technology. “Further research into Mycenaean combat technology will continue to illuminate details on the Late Bronze Age and the transition into the Iron Age,” researchers noted.
